findings.title: Spawn flusher processes are never killed or terminated
findings.body: Processes are created with multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process, but restart and shutdown only call kill()/terminate() when isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process). On Linux the default context Process class is the fork implementation, and SpawnProcess does not subclass it, so the check is false in production. A hung or crashed flusher is therefore left running while _create_process_for_shards starts another daemon on the same shards, and join() never signals the extras to exit. Those overlapping flushers both call flush_segments and produce the same segments to Kafka until the restart cap crashes the consumer, duplicating span data.

findings.title: Restart does not reap the old flusher before starting the next
findings.body: After a failed kill(), or even after a successful asynchronous kill()/SIGKILL, the old process object is overwritten without join(). The previous flusher can still be inside flush_segments/produce/done_flush_segments while the replacement process starts on the same shard list and Redis keys. Two flushers then emit the same segments, and unreaped children accumulate as zombies across the up-to-10 restarts.

findings.title: join() drops remaining flushers when the deadline hits
findings.body: join() walks processes and breaks as soon as remaining_time <= 0, before terminate() for that process or any later ones. The previous single-process join always terminated after the wait. With multiple flushers, a timeout therefore leaves later processes running (and, combined with the SpawnProcess isinstance check, never terminates them at all). Shutdown can return while those processes are still flushing and producing.

findings.title: Flusher metric tags are inconsistent and unbounded
findings.body: produce and segment_size_bytes are tagged with key "shard", but wait_produce uses "shards", so the two timers cannot be joined in the same dashboards. The value is ",".join of every shard on that process. With the CLI default of one flusher process that string is the full partition assignment, and it changes on every rebalance, creating a new high-cardinality series (and a very long tag) per assignment instead of a stable per-shard tag.

findings.title: Added sleep is a no-op under the time.sleep monkeypatch
findings.body: test_basic replaces time.sleep with a lambda that returns immediately, then calls time.sleep(0.1) to "give flusher threads time to process" after setting current_drift. That call is the patched function, so it does not wait. The flush still races with join(), which sets stopped immediately, so the test can pass or fail depending on thread scheduling and does not actually cover the timing it was changed to fix.
